Political Prison Camps (PPCs) are considered to be the most notorious detention facilities in North Korea. To this day the North Korean government denies the existence of the PPCs so it is very difficult to obtain information related to them. It is known that these detention facilities are under the control of Bureau 7 of the Ministry of State Security (MSS). Inside North Korea PPCs are called different names in order to conceal their nature. They are often called kwanliso (control centers) or kyohwaso, which is actually used for general prisons in North Korea. PPCs usually occupy large areas of land in mountainous regions. On the outside many PPCs look like villages and thus rarely cause suspicion even among people living near them.


In North Korea crimes deemed to be against the state and the nation are considered political crimes. Therefore, people who committed such acts are sent to PPCs. In North Korea there is no specific definition of a political crime and very often seemingly not serious offenses can be categorized as political crime. Moreover, not everybody who is sent to a PPC had actually committed a crime. North Korea implements a harsh system of guilt by association according to which several generations of family members can be punished for the crime of one person. Victims treated as political criminals are arrested, interrogated and then sent to a PPC without a proper trial. Upon entry at the PPC people are stripped off their citizenship and identification documents thus effectively losing all their rights as North Korean citizens. There is no official statistics available on the total number of political prisoners held in North Korea today. Estimates show that there are between 90,000 to 200,000 people held in PPCs in North Korea.


PPC in North Korea are divided into two areas called “total control zones” and “revolutionary zones”. People sent to total control zones are never released and after their death their bodies are buried in the camp. The crimes of such prisoners are considered so severe that they are treated as dangerous elements, who cannot be reeducated and reformed. At the same time people sent to revolutionary zones are considered a lesser threat to society and they are usually released after a certain period of time spent being reformed in the PPC. Unlike total control zones where no reeducation sessions are held, prisoners in revolutionary zones are subjected to multiple ideological lessons and self-criticism sessions. The majority of the information that the international community currently has on PPCs comes from the witness testimonies of people who have been released from revolutionary zones. Since the beginning of the 2010s all known revolutionary zones of PPC in North Korea has been dismantled and the remaining PPCs are managed as total control zones with little to no chance of escape of the people held there. As a result the latest data obtained on North Korean PPCs refers to detention conditions and violations of the same period since it is virtually impossible for prisoners in Total Control Zones to escape the camps. 


According to witness testimonies people sent in PPCs are treated in a most inhuman manner with no consideration of their dignity. Detainees are given very little food and no medical care while living in a highly unsanitary environment. They are forced to perform hard labor for hours on end at construction sites, mines and farms. Children are also mobilized to work alongside adults. Investigations on human rights perpetrated in PPCs show that executions, physical violence, torture, sexual abuse and ill-treatment of elderly people and children.


Although the exact number of PPCs in North Korea remains unknown NKDB’s research has revealed information on 15 such camps. Currently it is suspected that only three of them remain operational: Hwasong PPC No. 16, Yodok PPC No. 15, and Kaechon PPC No. 14. The international community does not exclude the possibility of the existence of new PPCs but without witness testimonies it is difficult to obtain information on new facilities.

Detention facilities are places used by North Korean security and judicial authorities to securely house individuals who are under investigation, undergoing a criminal trial, or serving a criminal sentence. In other places around the world, this would be akin to police holding cells (where suspects are held after arrest), jails (where suspects are held during court proceedings), and prisons (where convicted individuals are held after receiving their sentences). North Korea maintains a diverse range of similar facilities. It is estimated that there are hundreds of thousands of people currently detained across the country subjected to torture, forced labor and squalid conditions in these facilities. NKDB estimates that there are about 700 detention facilities throughout North Korea which can be categorized into seven types: political prison camp (kwan-li-so), prison (kyo-hwa-so), re-education detention facility (kyo-yang-so), police holding camp (jip-kyeol-so), labor training camp (ro-dong dan-ryeon-dae) as well as ‘other’ detention facilities such as psychiatric institutions, military detention facilities and detention facilities specifically created for foreigners. The basic temporary detention facility (gu-ryu-jang) is used to detain suspects who are undergoing trial and are managed by the Ministry of State Security or Ministry of People's Security, depending on the type of crime. There are also facilities referred to as police holding camps, or PHCs (jip-kyeol-so) and re-education camps(kyo-yang-so) which temporarily hold people in the border areas who have tried to escape to China or are have been caught traveling in another province without a verified travel permit. The more permanent facilities include prisons or correctional centers (kyo-hwa-so) where convicts serve their terms after having received their sentences, and the labor training camps (ro-dong dan-ryeon-dae), where many of the inmates still await the decision regarding the exact terms of their sentence. As of July 2020, NKDB Unified Human Rights Database has 30,057 cases of illegal detentions among a total of 78,798 cases of human rights violations.

North Korea remains one of about 50 countries in the world that are still effectively applying the death penalty. According to the DPRK Criminal Law as of the late 2010s there are 27 crimes punishable by death. The North Korean government has introduced some changes to its legislation to introduce lifelong imprisonment as an alternative to the death penalty in the case of some crimes. However, most of the definitions of the crimes punishable by the death penalty remain very vague, often involving a non-descript ‘anti-state activity’, and this leads to open interpretation and abuse of the text of the Criminal Law. Additionally, public executions have been used by the North Korean authorities to instill fear among citizens and thus prevent them from engaging in acts that are considered anti-state crimes. In North Korea such acts can be watching, listening to or reading foreign videos, music and books smuggled from outside the country, or trying to escape from North Korea to South Korea. In order to make stronger impact, North Korean authorities force a large portion of the local population (including children and adolescents) to be present and witness the public executions of accused persons. Public executions are usually held at stadiums, market places, deserted airfields, and other public spaces. Multiple records collected by NKDB reveal the witness accounts of North Korean people who were forced to watch public executions by firing squad or hanging, which was a truly traumatizing experience in their lives.


In the beginning of 2010s, the international community took a very strong stance about the application of the death penalty in the DPRK and more specifically the wide use of public executions for the purposes of political purges and control over the population. The 2014 UN Commission of Inquiry report concluded that “[a]lmost every citizen of the DPRK has become a witness to an execution.” As a result of international pressure and coordinated advocacy efforts the number of reported public executions has decreased since then. North Korea remains very concerned about its image in the world and has thus resorted to less visible alternative methods such as secret executions often perpetrated inside detention facilities. Collecting information on these violations is difficult and direct witness accounts are rarely available, which has made the effort to monitor the application of the death penalty and overall violations of the right to life in North Korea more complicated.

Cases of religious persecution are part of the larger category of violations of the right to freedom of belief and expression. Articles 18 of both the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights state that “everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion.” Although the DPRK is a state party to these conventions and the North Korean constitution includes a guarantee for citizens’ freedom of religion (Article 68), the reality in the country is very different. There is no actual freedom of religion in North Korea. The North Korean government has been suppressing all forms of free and independent expression, including the practice of religion. In North Korea, where idolization of the leader of the country takes priority over everything else, religion is viewed as a threat to the Kim family’s personality cult. Under the North Korean songbun caste system, religious people are given a corresponding number (ex. '37' for Protestants, '38' for Buddhists, and '39' for Catholics) and classified as ‘hostile.’ As a result of this, people who are suspected of proselytization of religion, praying, reading or just being in possession of the Bible are treated as political prisoners and punished severely often by detention in political prison camp or by public execution. As a result of the application of such policies of persecution North Korea has consistently been designated as “country of particular concern” by the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) and has been ranked as the worst oppressor to Christians by the organization Open Doors. 
To create the illusive image that freedom of religion exists in the country, the North Korean government maintains several religious facilities such as Catholic, Protestant, Eastern Orthodox and Chondoist churches and several Buddhist temples. However, these facilities are not open to the public and only foreigners residing in Pyongyang and a select number of North Koreans closely affiliated with the regime can access these facilities. The average North Korean citizens who have religious believes practice their faith in secret or in so called ‘underground churches’. According to data collected by Cornerstone International Ministries there were about 1,700 underground churches in North Korea as of 2015. Information on the practice of religion in the country is difficult to obtain since any religious activity is kept secret out of fear that people may get caught by the authorities or reported to them by other people. Activist groups active in China affiliated with churches and religious organizations based in South Korea or other countries, take great risks to smuggle Bibles inside North Korea and to support people of faith in the DPRK.

The North Korean government claims that there is full equality between men and women in North Korea and that women enjoy all basic rights and freedoms. In reality, research and witness testimonies show that women suffer many violations specific to them (sexual violence, forced abortions and human trafficking) and they are subjects to strong discrimination as a result of the patriarchal nature of the North Korean society.


When it comes to international treaties protecting the rights of women, North Korea ratified the Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) in 2001. Following this the DPRK took some legislative action to enhance the rights of North Korean women by enacting the Law on the Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Women in 2010. Despite the existing DPRK laws discrimination against women persists in North Korea. Gender-based violence is prevalent in society but there is little to no knowledge on this concept and people in North Korea accept it as almost a normal part of everyday life. According to surveys conducted by NKDB, women in the DPRK frequently experience domestic violence. Physical violence and sexual abuse on women are prominent in detention facilities such as prisons, interrogation facilities operated by the Ministry of State Security and police holding camps. Additionally, when it comes to political participation, women in North Korea are highly underrepresented in positions of power such as decision-making posts within the Korea Workers’ Party, Cabinet and the Supreme People’s Assembly. NKDB’s research shows that women in North Korea suffer from lack of proper medical care, which negatively affects their health and well-being. Although the rising importance of markets in the DPRK has led to an increased role of North Korea women as bread winners it has also created many difficulties for them. Women involved in the trade of goods are more likely to become victims of corruption, abuse of authority by government officials, and sexual violence and intimidation.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights stipulates many diverse types of freedom as important parts of human dignity. The right not to be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment (Article 5) is one of them. The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment on December 10th, 1984. Moreover, the 1993 Vienna Declaration clearly states that the ban on torture must be abided by at all times -even in warfare- and that a prompt acceding of United Nations member states to this Convention is called for. Despite international endeavors to ban torture, numerous different kinds of torture and physical violence are still perpetrated on people in North Korea.


Torture and physical assault are frequently committed on detainees and inmates in various detention facilities, including Political Prison Camps (PPC), Prisons, etc. Regarding the causes of the torture and physical violence cases, most causes of torture and physical violence are criminal offenses, followed by border management crimes. This is because North Korea’s security and law enforcement authorities rely on self-statements and confessions to prove the validity of the crimes if they do not have specific evidence.


In the 1990s, due to a large number of North Korean defectors crossing the Chinese border, many North Koreans were arrested as illegal immigrants by the Chinese police, detained in border detention facilities, and were subsequently tortured by the Chinese authorities. After being forcibly repatriated to North Korea, torture and physical violence mostly occurred in the process of investigating the motivations for the defection in the interrogation and detention facilities of the MSS and MPS, whether that may be contacting Christians or South Koreans, or attempting to defect to South Korea. Furthermore, torture and physical violence took place when people failed to follow regulations in prisons or detention facilities, or when new information was revealed.


Torture and physical violence are further divided into 24 types: Beating (Violence), Hanging, Physical Disablement or Bone Fractures, Burns, Rape, Sexual abuse and harassment, Exposure to Extreme Heat or Cold Environments, Electrocution, etc.
